title: Starting a Group Home for Children in North Dakota: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction (2-3 paragraphs):

Starting a Group Home for Children in North Dakota represents a meaningful opportunity to serve children requiring out-of-home placement, often with behavioral health needs or histories of trauma, while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS), specifically its Children and Family Services Licensing Unit. Reimbursement and program funding are coordinated through North Dakota Medicaid, particularly its Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) waiver programs.

With a growing market estimated to reach $33.5 million by 2025 and reimbursement rates around $10.70 per 15-minute behavioral health unit, North Dakota offers a specialized market with significant opportunity for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. The demand is particularly high for providers who can offer trauma-informed care and achieve Qualified Residential Treatment Program (QRTP) certification, addressing a critical need within the state’s child welfare system.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Group Home for Children in North Dakota, from understanding state and federal regulations to developing a business plan, hiring qualified staff, and preparing for your initial licensing inspection.

Table of Contents

  • Understand North Dakota’s Group Home for Children Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand North Dakota’s Group Home for Children Regulations

North Dakota regulates Group Homes for Children through the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS) Children and Family Services Licensing Unit, which is responsible for establishing and enforcing standards for safety, care, and program quality. The primary state-level regulations are found in the North Dakota Administrative Code (NDAC) 75-03-16. Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations must also comply with federal frameworks, most notably the Family First Prevention Services Act (FFPSA).

The regulatory framework emphasizes a strong focus on safety, trauma-informed care, behavioral health support, and compliance with both state and federal standards. This includes detailed requirements for resident rights, physical environment safety, staff-to-resident ratios, comprehensive documentation, and quality oversight. Licenses typically require renewal every one to two years, contingent upon successful compliance reviews and inspections.

Navigating these interconnected state and federal rules is the first and most critical step in your journey. Understanding the expectations of NDHHS and the requirements for QRTP certification will set the foundation for a successful application and a sustainable program.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

North Dakota supports multiple types of residential programs for children, each with different licensing, staffing, and reimbursement implications. Choosing the right model depends on your mission, expertise, and financial capacity. The market shows a clear preference for programs offering specialized, intensive services.

Key program variants include:

  • Basic Group Home: This model provides 24-hour supervision, shelter, and basic life skills support for children in a community-based setting. While essential, this model is becoming less common as the system shifts toward more intensive therapeutic interventions.
  • Therapeutic Group Home: This program integrates clinical services directly into the residential environment. It includes structured individual, group, and family therapy, overseen by licensed mental health professionals, to address significant behavioral and emotional challenges.
  • Qualified Residential Treatment Program (QRTP): This is a federally designated level of care under the Family First Act, representing the highest standard for residential treatment. QRTPs must be trauma-informed, employ a registered or licensed nursing and clinical staff, facilitate family outreach and inclusion, and provide comprehensive discharge planning. Achieving QRTP certification is a significant competitive advantage and is in high demand by state referral agencies.

Program size typically ranges from 4 to 12 residents, which allows for a more personalized and manageable therapeutic environment. Market data indicates that demand is strongest for specialized services in rural communities, which are often underserved. While urban centers may have more resources, they also feature more competition. Programs that can deliver high-quality, QRTP-certified care in rural regions are positioned to fill a critical gap.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can apply for a license, you must establish a formal business entity. Providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or a Corporation (S-Corp or C-Corp) to protect personal assets from business liabilities. Consult with a legal and financial advisor to determine the best structure for your situation.

To formalize your business and prepare for licensing, you must:

  • Register your business with the North Dakota Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and tax purposes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (errors and omissions), and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the NDHHS Children and Family Services Licensing Unit. This application will require detailed information about your program, facility, finances, staffing plan, and policies and procedures.

Licensing timelines in North Dakota generally range from 6 to 12 months. This timeframe is highly dependent on the completeness of your application, your readiness for the facility inspection, and the agency’s current processing volume. A thorough and well-prepared application is key to avoiding delays.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to a compliant and financially viable group home. It is essential for securing funding and guiding your operational decisions. Startup costs in North Dakota typically range from $200,000 to $1,000,000, covering facility acquisition or renovation, licensing fees, insurance, initial payroll, and operational reserves.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which represents approximately 60-70% of total costs due to the need for 24/7 supervision and specialized clinical roles. Your financial projections must be grounded in the state’s reimbursement structure.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in North Dakota include:

  • Per-Unit Reimbursement: Funding through Medicaid HCBS waivers is often calculated in units. For example, behavioral health services may be reimbursed at approximately $10.70 per 15-minute unit.
  • Annual Revenue: Depending on licensed capacity, service intensity (especially for QRTPs), and occupancy rates, a group home can generate between $500,000 and $3,000,000 in annual revenue.

Profitability is closely tied to occupancy. Providers operating at a target occupancy of around 60-65% generally achieve 10-15% profit margins. Your business plan should include a break-even analysis, which for this sector is often projected at 12-18 months post-licensure.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

The physical location of your group home is a critical component of your license. The facility must not only be safe and comfortable but also meet the specific requirements outlined in NDAC 75-03-16. Your choice of location should consider local zoning ordinances, proximity to schools and community resources, accessibility for families, and the availability of a qualified workforce.

Key facility requirements include:

  • Compliance with Local Codes: The building must pass inspections for local zoning, building, fire, and health codes.
  • Adequate Bedroom Space: Each resident must have a designated bed and personal space, with limitations on the number of residents per room.
  • Sufficient Bathroom Facilities: The home must have an adequate number of clean and accessible toilets, sinks, and showers for residents and staff.
  • Common Areas: The facility needs designated spaces for dining, recreation, and therapeutic activities.
  • A Secure and Clean Environment: The home must be well-maintained, free of hazards, and provide a safe and sanitary living environment.
  • Administrative Space: A private office is required for administrative tasks, storing confidential records, and staff meetings.
  • Accessibility: The facility should be accessible to individuals with physical disabilities, in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your program. The quality of care you provide is directly related to the qualifications, training, and dedication of your team. NDHHS has stringent requirements for staffing ratios, background checks, and qualifications.

Required roles for a group home for children typically include:

  • Program Director/Administrator: An experienced professional who oversees all administrative and programmatic operations, ensuring compliance with all state and federal regulations.
  • Clinical Supervisor (for therapeutic/QRTP models): A licensed mental health professional (e.g., LCSW, LPC) who provides clinical oversight, supervises therapeutic staff, and guides treatment planning.
  • Direct Care Staff / Youth Counselors: These individuals provide 24/7 supervision, mentorship, and daily support to residents. They are the frontline of your program.
  • Case Manager: Responsible for coordinating services, developing individual care plans, and acting as the primary liaison with state agencies, schools, and families.
  • Therapist/Clinician: If providing services in-house, a licensed therapist is needed to deliver individual, group, and family therapy as outlined in each resident’s treatment plan.

All staff must undergo rigorous background checks. Training is non-negotiable and must be documented. Key training requirements include Trauma-Informed Care, Crisis Prevention and Intervention (e.g., CPI), First Aid/CPR, Medication Administration, and Mandatory Reporting of child abuse and neglect. Ongoing continuing education is also mandated to ensure staff skills remain current.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Written policies and procedures are the operational backbone of your group home. They demonstrate to the NDHHS that you have a clear, compliant plan for every aspect of your operation. These documents will be meticulously reviewed during your licensing inspection.

North Dakota requires written policies covering, at a minimum:

  • Admissions and Discharge Criteria: Clear guidelines on the population you serve and the process for intake and planned discharge.
  • Resident Rights and Grievance Procedures: A formal process for protecting resident rights and addressing complaints.
  • Behavior Management and De-escalation: A trauma-informed approach to managing challenging behaviors that prioritizes safety and avoids punitive measures.
  • Medication Management and Administration: Strict protocols for storing, administering, and documenting all medications.
  • Emergency and Disaster Preparedness: A detailed plan for handling fires, medical emergencies, severe weather, and other crises.
  • Staffing, Training, and Supervision: Policies outlining hiring qualifications, training requirements, staff scheduling, and supervision.
  • Health and Safety Protocols: Procedures for infection control, accident prevention, and maintaining a safe physical environment.
  • Record-Keeping and Confidentiality: Protocols for maintaining secure, confidential resident and staff records in compliance with HIPAA.
  • Family Engagement and Communication: A plan for involving family in the treatment process, as required for QRTP certification.

In addition to these organizational policies, individual care or service plans must be developed for each resident. These plans must be person-centered, created in collaboration with the child’s treatment team and family, and regularly reviewed and updated per state and federal rules.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Marketing a group home for children is fundamentally different from other businesses. Success does not come from consumer advertising but from building trust and demonstrating compliance with key referral agencies. Your reputation for providing high-quality, reliable care is your most powerful marketing tool.

Referrals in North Dakota will almost exclusively come from:

  • North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS) social workers and case managers.
  • Juvenile court systems and probation officers.
  • Tribal social service agencies serving children within their jurisdictions.
  • School districts seeking specialized residential placements for students with significant behavioral needs.

To build these crucial relationships, focus on proactive communication, flawless compliance during surveys, and positive outcomes for the children in your care. Attend provider meetings, introduce your program director to regional agency leadership, and be responsive and transparent in all your communications. Your ability to accept placements efficiently and manage complex cases will make you a preferred provider.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Ongoing oversight is conducted by the NDHHS Children and Family Services Licensing Unit, which performs regular and unannounced inspections. For QRTP-certified programs, an independent assessment body will also be involved in reviews.

Inspections are comprehensive and focus on ensuring adherence to all regulations. Surveyors will review resident records, staff files, medication logs, and the physical environment. Common deficiencies often cited include:

  • Incomplete or outdated resident records and treatment plans.
  • Lapses in staff training documentation or certifications.
  • Errors in medication administration or storage.
  • Environmental hazards, such as blocked exits or sanitation issues.
  • Failure to consistently follow the program’s own written policies and procedures.

To maintain compliance, implement a robust continuous quality improvement (CQI) program. Conduct regular self-audits of your files and facility to catch and correct potential issues before a surveyor finds them. Keeping your documentation audit-ready at all times is essential for a smooth survey and long-term operational success.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a Group Home for Children in North Dakota?

A: The entire process, from business planning to receiving your first placement, can take 12 to 18 months. This includes securing a facility, completing the extensive licensing application with the NDHHS, hiring staff, and passing inspections.

Q: What licenses are required?

A: You need a license from the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS) Children and Family Services Licensing Unit, governed by North Dakota Administrative Code 75-03-16. For higher levels of care, a Qualified Residential Treatment Program (QRTP) certification is also highly recommended to meet market demand and federal standards.

Q: What reimbursement is available?

A: Reimbursement primarily comes from North Dakota Medicaid through its Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) waiver programs. Rates are often structured in units, such as approximately $10.70 per 15-minute unit for behavioral health services. Total revenue depends on your facility’s capacity, occupancy, and the intensity of services provided.

Conclusion:

Starting a Group Home for Children in North Dakota is a challenging but deeply rewarding venture. It requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and a steadfast commitment to operational discipline. The market has a clear need for specialized providers who can deliver trauma-informed, clinically sophisticated care, particularly those who achieve QRTP certification. Providers who invest in compliance, high-quality staffing, and strong relationships with state referral agencies are positioned for long-term success and a meaningful impact on the lives of vulnerable children.
